tagline: A short avenue through the town that expected to be capital.
intro: Inside the Marshall city limits Michigan Avenue becomes the byway, a mile and a fifth of shops and landmarks through a National Historic Landmark district of more than 850 buildings. The road carries 28 historical markers, more than any Michigan town outside Detroit.

Marshall expected to be the state capital and built a house for the governor to prove it. The vote went to Lansing. In 1847 the town did something less expected: when slave catchers came for Adam Crosswhite and his family, a crowd of over 100 turned out, gave the Kentuckians their names and spelled them, and hid the family in a mill attic until a wagon could carry them off to the Detroit train.

moments.title: Honolulu House
moments.text: Abner Pratt came home from the consulate in Hawaii and in 1860 built himself a piece of it, with a wraparound veranda, tropical scenes on the walls and a pagoda tower over the door.

moments.title: Fountain Circle
moments.text: The Brooks Memorial Fountain copies the Temple of Love from Marie Antoinette's garden, and the National House Inn of 1835, the oldest operating inn in Michigan, looks out on it.

moments.title: Governor's Mansion
moments.text: Built in 1839 for a governor who never came, it now belongs to the local chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution.
